title: Working back from the end
objectives: Solve pirate and voting puzzles by backward induction from the smallest case.

screens.title: Sixty coins
screens.prose: Pirates A, B, C and D rank from A down. The most senior alive proposes a split of 60 coins, and everyone alive votes, proposer included. At least half voting yes passes it; otherwise he goes overboard. Each wants to survive, then coins, then to see others thrown over.

state.caption: If A's split fails, B proposes to three. If that fails, C proposes to two. Offered only what he would get anyway, a pirate votes no.

screens.question: Fill in each pirate's coins with 3 aboard and with 4 aboard.

hints.text: Start at 2 aboard: C's own vote is half, so he keeps all 60.
With 3 aboard, B needs one vote besides his own. Who gets 0 if B fails?
3 aboard: B 59, C 0, D 1. With 4 aboard, C gets 0 under B, so A buys C for 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve 2 aboard, then 3, then 4, each time asking what a failure gives.

byKey.r1c2: B needs only one vote besides his own, and D's costs 1 coin. B keeps 59.
byKey.r3c2: D gets 0 if B goes overboard, so 1 coin beats that. 0 would not buy him.
byKey.r0c3: A needs one vote besides his own, and C's costs 1. A keeps 59.
byKey.r2c3: C gets 0 under B, so 1 coin buys C. He is the cheapest vote.

explain.text: With 2 aboard C keeps all 60, since his own vote is half. With 3, D gets 0 if B fails, so 1 coin buys him: (59, 0, 1). With 4, C gets 0 under B, so A pays C 1: (59, 0, 1, 0).

screens.title: The cheapest vote
screens.prose: Four aboard again. A needs one vote besides his own. Each vote costs one coin more than its owner gets if A goes overboard.

state.caption: Under B, with 3 aboard: B 59, C 0, D 1.

screens.question: Whose vote does A buy?

options.why: B gets 59 under his own split, so his vote costs 60 and A would keep nothing.
D gets 1 under B, so 1 coin is no better. His vote costs 2.
Two votes of four is half, so A needs only one besides his own.

hints.text: Read each pirate's coins under B from the tree.
C gets 0 under B.
C's price is 0 + 1 = 1, the lowest.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each vote at what its owner gets under B, plus one.

byKey.b: B gets 59 if A goes over, so he wants 60. That leaves A nothing.
byKey.d: D gets 1 under B. Offered 1 he votes no, since he also enjoys seeing A thrown over.
byKey.all: Half the votes pass it, and A's own vote is one of the two.

explain.text: Under B, C gets 0, D gets 1 and B gets 59. So the prices are 1 for C, 2 for D and 60 for B. A buys the cheapest: C for 1 coin.

screens.title: Seven lions
screens.prose: Seven lions share an island with one sheep. A lion that eats the sheep falls asleep and becomes a sheep, which another lion may eat. Every lion would rather live than eat, but eats whenever it is safe. Work back from one lion.

state.caption: Each step right: a lion has eaten, and one fewer lion is awake.

screens.question: Does the first lion eat the sheep?

options.text: No: whoever eats is eaten next
options.why: That is true with 2 lions. With 6 left awake, nobody dares eat, so the sleeper is safe.

options.text: No: with seven lions, someone always eats the sleeper
options.why: You assumed some lion always eats. Work back: with an even number awake, none does.

hints.text: One lion eats safely. What about two?
With 2 lions, an eater is eaten by the other, so neither eats.
1 eats, 2 wait, 3 eat, and so on: odd numbers eat.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide 1, 2 and 3 lions, then spot the pattern.

byKey.no-eaten: With 7 lions, an eater leaves 6 awake, and 6 lions do not eat. So it is safe.
byKey.no-many: Work back: 2 lions wait, 4 wait, 6 wait. With 6 awake, the sleeper survives.

explain.text: One lion eats; two wait, since an eater would be eaten. Three eat, leaving the safe case of two, and so on. Seven is odd, so the first lion eats: work back from the smallest case.

screens.title: An equal split
screens.prose: Back to A, B, C and D with 60 coins. A candidate says A must be generous to survive: 15 each, so that all four vote yes.

state.caption: Under B, with 3 aboard: B 59, C 0, D 1.

screens.question: How many coins does A keep?

options.why: You gave everyone the same. B votes no to 15, since he gets 59 if A goes over.

options.text: Very few: the others gang up on him
options.why: You guessed the senior is weak. He needs only one vote, and C's costs 1 coin.

options.text: 30: he pays half to win a vote
options.why: You overpaid. C gets 0 under B, so 1 coin is enough.

hints.text: What does each pirate get if A goes overboard?
Under B, C gets 0.
A buys C for 1 and keeps 59.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each vote from the 3-aboard game.

byKey.15: An equal split loses B's vote and wastes coins on D. A needs only C, for 1.
byKey.few: Backward induction gives the senior pirate the most. He keeps 59.
byKey.30: C's price is what he gets under B, which is 0, plus one.

explain.text: The equal split ignores what each pirate gets if A fails. C gets 0 under B, so 1 coin buys C, and A keeps 59. Principle: price every vote by the next game, not by fairness.

screens.title: Merciful pirates
screens.prose: Change one preference. Now a pirate offered what he would get anyway votes yes, out of mercy. Everything else stays the same.
screens.question: Which is true for merciful pirates and 60 coins?

options.text: The proposer keeps all 60 for every crew size
The splits are the same as before
options.why: Mercy changes the price. A vote now costs what its owner gets next, with no extra coin.

options.text: The proposer keeps 59 once 3 are aboard
options.why: That pays 1 coin a vote. Merciful pirates who get 0 next vote yes for 0.

hints.text: With 3 aboard, what does D get if B fails?
D gets 0 after B fails, and now 0 buys him.
Every bought vote costs 0, so the proposer keeps 60.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each vote at what its owner gets next, with no extra coin.

byKey.same: Before, D wanted 1 coin to beat 0. Now 0 already buys him.
byKey.59: With mercy, a pirate who gets 0 next accepts 0, so no coin is spent.

explain.text: With 2 aboard C keeps 60, and D gets 0. With 3, D accepts 0, so B keeps 60, and each larger crew has someone who gets 0 next. Principle: change the tie rule and the whole induction changes.

screens.title: Back from the end
screens.prose: Each time we solved the smallest crew first, then each larger crew knowing what follows a failure. That is **backward induction**. $$\text{price of a vote} = \text{coins after a failure} + 1$$ Zhou's green book (its brainteasers chapter), Crack's *Heard on the Street* and Joshi and co-authors all set such puzzles.
screens.question: With 5 aboard, how many votes must A buy besides his own?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At least half of 5 is 3 votes, his own included.

byKey.three: Three votes is at least half, and A's own vote is one of them. He buys two.
byKey.four: A needs at least half, not everyone. Three votes of five is enough.
byKey.one: Two votes of five is less than half. He needs three, his own and two more.

explain.text: At least half of 5 means 3 votes, and A's own is one. So he buys two, the cheapest two after a failure. Take-away games follow in Probability Puzzles, and bargaining in Games, Auctions and Poker.

screens.title: A rule for every crew
screens.prose: The proposer keeps 60 with 2 aboard, 59 with 3 or 4, and 58 with 5 or 6. Each extra pair of pirates costs one more coin.
screens.question: Which formula gives the proposer's coins with $n$ aboard, for $n$ from 2 to 10?

options.why: That buys a vote from all but one of the others. Only the pirates who get 0 next are bought, every second one.
Check $n = 2$: that gives 59, but C keeps all 60.
That is the equal split, which loses votes.

hints.text: Test each formula at $n = 2, 3, 4, 5$.
$\lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ is 0, 1, 1, 2 for $n = 2, 3, 4, 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each formula against 60, 59, 59, 58.

byKey.lin: At $n = 4$ that gives 58, but A keeps 59.
byKey.eq: An equal split is never the answer here.

explain.text: With $n$ aboard the proposer needs $\lceil n/2 \rceil - 1 = \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$ votes besides his own. Each costs 1 coin, from the pirates who get 0 next. So he keeps $60 - \lfloor (n-1)/2 \rfloor$, which a full search confirms up to 10.

screens.title: Drill: five pirates
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Five pirates, 60 coins, the same rules as at the start.
screens.question: How many coins does the proposer keep?

hints.text: He needs two votes besides his own.
With 4 aboard the split is (59, 0, 1, 0).
Pirates 3 and 5 of the five get 0 next, so 1 coin each: (58, 0, 1, 0, 1).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price each vote from the 4-aboard game.

byKey.59: Two votes are needed besides his own: 3 of 5 is at least half.
byKey.12: An equal split loses the votes of pirates who would do better next.
byKey.57: You bought three votes. Three of five, his own included, is enough.

explain.text: Under the 4-aboard split (59, 0, 1, 0), the second and fourth of those four get 0. They are the third and fifth of the five, so 1 coin each buys them. The proposer keeps 58: (58, 0, 1, 0, 1).

screens.title: Drill: six pirates
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Six pirates, 60 coins, the same rules.
screens.question: How many coins does the proposer keep?

hints.text: Three votes of six is half.
With 5 aboard the split is (58, 0, 1, 0, 1).
Two pirates get 0 there, so the proposer buys them: (58, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Three votes of six is half; buy two.

byKey.57: Half of six is three votes, so he buys two, not three.
byKey.10: An equal split ignores what each pirate gets next.
byKey.59: One bought vote makes two of six, which is less than half.

explain.text: Three votes of six is half, so he buys two. In the 5-aboard split two pirates get 0, and 1 coin each buys them. He keeps 58: (58, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0).

screens.title: Drill: ten lions
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Ten lions and one sheep, the same rules as the seven lions.
screens.question: Does the first lion eat the sheep?

options.text: Yes: there are plenty of lions to protect it
options.why: More lions do not protect an eater. With 9 left awake, one of them eats it.

options.text: Only if it is the hungriest
options.why: Every lion reasons the same way; only the count matters.

hints.text: Odd numbers of lions eat.
If the first eats, 9 lions are awake.
Nine is odd, so a lion would eat the sleeper.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lions left awake after the first eats.

byKey.yes: Eating leaves 9 awake, and with 9 one lion eats. So the first waits.
byKey.depends: Hunger does not enter. The parity of the count decides.

explain.text: If the first lion eats, 9 remain awake with a sleeping sheep. Nine is odd, so one of them eats it. Ten is even, so the first lion waits: parity of the count decides.

screens.title: Drill: forty coins
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. Three pirates and 40 coins, the same rules.
screens.question: How many coins does the proposer keep?

hints.text: With 2 aboard, the senior keeps all 40.
The junior pirate gets 0 there.
1 coin buys him: (39, 0, 1).

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One vote is needed, and the junior pirate's costs 1.

byKey.40: Offered 0, the junior votes no: he gets 0 anyway and enjoys a throw.
byKey.38: Two of three votes is enough, so he buys one, not two.
byKey.13: An equal split gives away coins nobody needs.

explain.text: With 2 aboard the senior of the two keeps 40, so the junior gets 0. The proposer buys the junior for 1 coin and keeps 39. Principle: the count of coins changes the numbers, not the method.

screens.title: More than half
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer now needs more than half to vote yes. With 2 aboard, D votes no, so C goes overboard and D keeps 60. A committee vote works the same way: price each vote by what its holder gets if the motion fails.
screens.question: Fill in the splits with 3 aboard and with 4 aboard.

hints.text: With 3 aboard, B needs two votes. What happens to C if B fails?
C goes overboard if B fails, so C votes yes for nothing.
3 aboard: (60, 0, 0). With 4 aboard A needs three votes; C and D get 0 under B, so 1 each.

feedback.correct: (60, 0, 0) with three aboard and (58, 0, 1, 1) with four.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With more than half needed, ask who dies if a proposal fails.

byKey.r1c2: C votes yes for 0 to stay alive, so B keeps all 60.
byKey.r2c2: C would drown if B failed, so he takes 0 and votes yes.
byKey.r3c2: D wants B gone, since he then keeps 60, but B does not need him.
byKey.r0c3: A needs three votes of four, so he buys two: C and D, at 1 each.

explain.text: With 3 aboard, C dies if B fails, so C votes yes for nothing: (60, 0, 0). With 4, A pays C and D 1 coin each, since both get 0 under B. Principle: survival can buy a vote more cheaply than coins.

ideas: Solve the smallest case first, then each larger case knowing what follows a failure.
A vote costs one coin more than its owner gets after a failure; buy the cheapest.
Change one rule, such as the tie or the majority, and redo the whole induction.

formula.name: Proposer's share
formula.note: At least half to pass, bloodthirsty pirates, $n$ from 2 to 10.

summary.trap: An equal split loses votes: the senior pirate keeps 59 of 60 with four aboard.

quiz.prose: Seven pirates share 60 coins. The most senior alive proposes, and everyone aboard votes, proposer included. At least half yes passes; otherwise he goes overboard. Each wants to live, then coins, then to see others thrown over.
quiz.question: How many coins does the proposer keep?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With 7 aboard he buys three votes at 1 coin each.

byKey.58: Four votes of seven is at least half, so he buys three, not two.
byKey.56: You bought four votes. Four of seven, his own included, is enough.

explain.text: At least half of 7 is 4 votes, so he buys three. Three pirates get 0 in the 6-aboard game, so 1 coin each. He keeps $60 - 3 = 57$.

quiz.prose: Five pirates, A to E from the most senior, share 60 coins. The most senior alive proposes, and everyone aboard votes, proposer included. At least half yes passes; otherwise he goes overboard. Each wants to live, then coins, then to see others thrown over.
quiz.question: Which pirates receive a coin from A? Select all that apply.

options.why: B gets 59 if A fails, so his vote is the dearest.
D gets 1 under B, so his vote costs 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find who gets 0 in the 4-aboard game under B.

byKey.b: B would propose next and keep 59. His vote is far too dear.
byKey.d: Under B, D gets 1 coin, so he costs 2.

explain.text: Under B the four-aboard split is (59, 0, 1, 0) for B, C, D and E. C and E get 0, so 1 coin each buys them. A keeps 58.

quiz.prose: Four lions and one sheep. A lion that eats the sheep falls asleep and becomes a sheep. Every lion would rather live than eat, but eats whenever it is safe.
quiz.question: Does the first lion eat the sheep?

options.why: If it eats, 3 lions are awake, and with 3 one of them eats it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lions left awake after an eater falls asleep.

byKey.yes: Three awake lions mean one eats the sleeper, so the first does not eat.

explain.text: If the first eats, 3 remain awake, and an odd number eats. So the first lion waits. Four is even.

quiz.prose: Three merciful pirates, B, C and D, share 60 coins: a pirate offered what he gets anyway votes yes.
quiz.question: How many coins does B give D?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. D gets 0 if B fails, and mercy makes 0 enough.

byKey.one: That is the price for bloodthirsty pirates. Merciful D accepts 0.

explain.text: If B fails, C keeps all 60 and D gets 0. Merciful D votes yes for 0, so B keeps all 60. The tie rule sets the price.
